name: Kalpavriksha (Wish-Fulfilling Tree)
era: Vedic; codified in Puranas (1st millennium CE)
story: The Kalpavriksha stands in the garden of the gods (the paradise of Indra) and grants the wishes of whoever approaches it. It bears every fruit, flower, and jewel; it is the source of all prosperity and the object of pilgrimage. In the Ramayana, Sita plants a wish-fulfilling tree in the Ashoka grove of Lanka, and the tree becomes a symbol of the paradise restored.
history: The Kalpavriksha is a central Puranic and Vedic concept — the tree that fulfills every desire. It appears in the Vishnu Purana, the Bhagavata Purana, and the Ramayana. Its iconography (a jeweled tree in a paradisiacal garden) became a standard motif of Indian painting and temple sculpture, and it is the direct ancestor of the 'tree of paradise' in South and Southeast Asian art.
details: The Kalpavriksha is the 'tree of life' as abundance: the source of every desire, every season, and every blessing. It is the cosmic garden's heart, the axis of prosperity, and the prototype of the paradise-tree that traveled with Buddhism and Hinduism across Asia.

name: Bodhi Tree (Ashvattha / Pippala)
story: Beneath a pippal (bodhi) tree in Bodh Gaya, the prince Siddhartha Gautama sat and resolved not to rise until he had awakened. There, through the night, he attained enlightenment (bodhi) and became the Buddha. The tree became the tree of awakening, and its leaves and shade are the enduring symbol of liberation, wisdom, and the path to enlightenment.
history: The original bodhi tree is said to have been planted in the 3rd c. BCE (from a cutting of the original) and stands today in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka (Sri Maha Bodhi), one of the oldest continuously tended trees in the world. The bodhi tree became the central icon of Buddhist art across Asia — the tree under which the Buddha sits, the tree of the stupa, and the tree of the mandala.
details: The bodhi tree is the 'tree of life' as awakening: the organism under which ignorance ends and wisdom begins. It encodes the tree as the seat of liberation, the source of insight, and the living teacher. Its iconography (Buddha under a heart-shaped-canopied tree) is the most recognizable 'tree of life' in the Buddhist world.

name: Ashvattha of the Bhagavad Gita
story: In the Bhagavad Gita (15.1-6), Krishna describes the eternal tree of existence: an ashvattha whose roots reach up (into the spirit) and whose branches reach down (into the world), whose leaves are the Vedic hymns. This tree is the tree of samsara — the world of birth and death. One must cut this tree with the 'axe of non-attachment' to reach the supreme abode from which, once attained, one is never again born.
history: The Gita's ashvattha is one of the most philosophically dense tree-images in world literature. It inverts the 'tree of life' into the 'tree of bondage' — the organism of cyclic existence that must be cut through to reach liberation. It is a direct counter-image to the Kalpavriksha and a key text for the Indian 'tree of life' tradition.
details: The ashvattha of the Gita is the tree of life as samsara: the inverted tree of desire and rebirth. Its 'upward roots, downward branches' and 'Vedic leaves' make it a cosmological map. It is the 'tree of life' turned into a map of bondage and the discipline needed to transcend it.

name: Ashoka Tree (Indian / Buddhist)
story: The Ashoka tree (the 'tree without sorrow') is the tree of the Emperor Ashoka and of the Buddhist paradise. It is the tree under which the Buddha's mother, Queen Maya, conceived him (in Jataka tradition), and it marks the sites of the Buddha's miracles. Its blossoms (a cascade of red-orange) are the flower of the 'paradise without sorrow' that bears the emperor's name.
history: The Ashoka tree is a shared sacred motif of Zoroastrian, Indian, and Buddhist traditions. In Buddhist art it is the 'tree of the miracle' and the 'paradise tree,' appearing in the stupa and in the garden of the Buddha's mother. Its name (a-soka, 'without sorrow') and its image traveled with Buddhism across Asia, becoming a standard icon of the paradise-tree.
details: The Ashoka is the 'tree of life' as the paradise without sorrow: the tree of the miracle, the tree of the Buddha's mother, and the tree of the emperor's renunciation. It is a key node in the cross-cultural genealogy of the paradise-tree, linking the Iranian, Indian, and Buddhist traditions.

name: Tala (Palm) of Nirvana
story: Between two sal-trees (or, in some traditions, two tala palms) at Kusinara, the Buddha attained parinirvana — his final passing beyond the cycle of rebirth. The tree marks the endpoint of the path, the place where the last of the Buddha's existences ended. The sal and tala become the 'trees of the final release.'
history: The tala/sal of the Buddha's parinirvana is one of the four great sacred sites of Buddhism (Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kusinara). The 'tree of nirvana' is a standard icon of Buddhist art — the sal grove of the passing, the tree that marks the end of samsara. It completes the Buddhist tree-cycle: the bodhi (awakening) and the tala (release).
details: The tala is the 'tree of life' as release: the organism that marks the end of the cycle of birth and death. It is the complement to the bodhi tree — the tree of awakening (the beginning of the path) and the tree of nirvana (the end of the path). Together they enclose the whole Buddhist journey.

name: Banyan of the Vedic World (Vat)
story: The banyan (vat) is the 'tree of the world' in Vedic and Hindu tradition — the vast, spreading tree whose aerial roots become new trunks, so that one tree is a grove. It is the tree of the world-tree, the organism that contains the whole cosmos in its spreading canopy and root-network. It is the 'world tree' of the Indian subcontinent.
history: The banyan is the national and sacred tree of India, attested from the Vedic period. Its 'one tree, many trunks' morphology made it the natural image of the world-tree, the mandala, and the cosmic order (rita). It is the living icon of the 'tree that is the world,' and it anchors the Indian world-tree tradition.
details: The banyan is the 'tree of life' as the world itself: the organism whose spreading roots and canopies are a map of the cosmos. It is the Indian axis mundi, the tree that contains heaven and earth in its body, and the living prototype of the mandala and the world-tree.

name: Mango Tree of the Gods
story: The mango is the 'king of fruits' and the tree of abundance in Hindu tradition. It is the tree of the gods' garden, the tree of love (associated with the god of love, Manmatha), and the tree of the harvest. Its fruit is the offering, its shade the refuge, and its blossom the flower of prosperity and love.
history: The mango is the sacred and national fruit-tree of India, attested from the Vedic period and central to Hindu ritual and art. It is the tree of abundance, the tree of love, and the 'tree of life' as nourishment and fertility. Its iconography (the mango grove, the offering of the fruit) is a standard of Indian painting.
details: The mango is the 'tree of life' as nourishment and love: the tree of the harvest, the tree of the gods, and the tree of the beloved. It encodes the tree as the source of the body's sustenance and of the heart's desire — the 'tree of life' in its most sensual and domesticated form.

name: Soma Tree (Vedic)
tree: Soma (possibly ephedra or a sacred shrub)
story: Soma is the sacred, life-giving plant of the Vedic ritual, whose pressed juice (soma) is drunk by the priests to grant vitality, inspiration, and immortality. The god Soma is the divine source of the nectar, and the 'tree' of soma is the source of the gods' vitality and of the prophet's revelation. It is the Indian counterpart of the Iranian Haoma.
history: Soma is central to the Rigveda (the Soma hymns) and is the Vedic counterpart of the Iranian Haoma. Its ritual pressing and drinking is one of the oldest continuous liturgical acts in the Indian world. The plant's identity is debated (ephedra, or a lost species), but its role as the divine tree of nectar and revelation is unambiguous.
details: As the 'tree of nectar,' Soma/Haoma links the tree of life to revelation, inspiration, and divine vitality — a theme echoed across the Indo-European world (the Greek kykeon, the Norse mead of poetry, the Christian Eucharist). It is the tree that gives humans the gods' own life.
